5. Historical Data Collection

The observed time series are based on data from instruments on satellites that collect images that can be used to generate weekly maps of snow cover. Data are collected for the entire Northern Hemisphere. Data were compiled as part of NOAA’s IMS, which incorporates imagery from a variety of satellite instruments (e.g., Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer [AVHRR], Geostationary Satellite Server [GOES], Special Sensor Microwave Imager [SSMI]) as well as derived mapped products and surface observations. The technical documentation for the Snow Cover indicator provides more information with links to peer-reviewed methodology papers and satellite mission descriptions.

6. Indicator Derivation

This feature involves calculating the total area of all grid cells on a map that are at least 50 percent snow-covered. Seasonal averaging uses meteorological seasons:

  • Winter: December (of the prior calendar year), January, and February.
  • Spring: March, April, and May.
  • Summer: June, July, and August.
  • Fall: September, October, and November.

Observed Data

NOAA digitized satellite maps weekly using the National Meteorological Center Limited-Area Fine Mesh grid. Rutgers University’s GSL reanalyzed the digitized maps produced by NOAA to correct for biases in the data set caused by locations of land masses and bodies of water that NOAA’s land mask does not completely resolve. GSL also applied a higher-resolution grid, with 24-kilometer resolution. The technical documentation for the Snow Cover indicator provides links to publications and websites that describe processing steps and reprocessing improvements. Of particular note, this analysis aggregates the total area of all grid cells that have at least 50 percent snow cover.

Weekly estimates were averaged to determine seasonal and annual averages. The project team converted all of these value from square kilometers to square miles to make the results accessible to a wider audience.

Model Outputs

The project team performed the following steps via R scripts:

  • The team analyzed monthly model outputs, or, in the case of two models that provide daily outputs, aggregated them to monthly for consistency with the other models.
  • For each model, the project team used the monthly “snc” variable to identify the proportion of each grid cell covered by snow, multiplied this proportion by each grid cell’s full area (CMIP6’s “areacella” variable), and then aggregated snow-covered area across North America (excluding Greenland).
  • The team aggregated the 13 models using a modified version of the Bayesian model weighting approach used in the Fifth National Climate Assessment and documented by Massoud et al. (2023). Because the standard weighting is based on 16 models, the authors of Massoud et al. (2023) provided corresponding weights for the subset of 13 models used here.
  • The team smoothed modeled results using an 11-year moving average. The team performed this step independently for the hindcast (through 2014) and for each scenario from 2015 (the first year of divergence) forward.

7. Alignment

The project team began this effort with the historical data set that appeared in EPA’s Snow Cover indicator. However, this data set showed a lack of alignment with model outputs. Upon discussion with GSL, the project team learned that they had developed a new product based on a higher-resolution gridded analysis. The resolution difference is sizable: each cell in the original published analysis had a resolution range of 16,000 to 42,000 square kilometers, compared with a nominal 576 square kilometers (24 x 24 kilometers) for the newer version. Figure TD-1 shows that switching to the new grid closed much of the gap between observations and projections for annual average snow cover. The same was true for seasonal averages.

Figure TD-1. Snow cover alignment: Changing observed resolution

Even after switching to the new observed data set, there was still a sizable gap between observations and projections, and that gap widened once the newest model selection and weighting was applied. (Figure TD-1 shows an earlier weighting.) Figure TD-2 shows the newer gap on the annual graph.

Figure TD-2. Snow cover alignment: Remaining gap requiring bias correction

The gap could have multiple explanations, including the models’ ability to project snow cover, the difference in grid cell size for analysis, and an associated difference in indicator methods. Regarding grid cell size, the GCM grid cells are much larger than the observed analysis’s grid cells, which precluded adoption of the observed analysis’s 50 percent yes/no criterion and associated “all or nothing” inclusion. With much larger grid cells in the model outputs, the project team determined that it would be more appropriate to count actual modeled snow-covered area than to risk including or excluding large areas in their entirety based on a threshold applied over a large and potentially heterogeneous spatial domain. In particular, the project team wanted to avoid overlooking modest expanses of snow cover that might have registered in the observed analysis but would not meet the 50 percent threshold in a much larger GCM grid cell. This could be a particular concern for summer.

The fact that improving the resolution of the observed data set demonstrably reduced the gap between observed and modeled snow area suggests in general that some type of bias is likely the cause of the observed gap. Thus, it is reasonable to expect that a bias correction would be an appropriate way to close the remaining gap. The project team applied a straightforward “delta method” additive bias correction to do so. The project team shifted all GCM outputs (hindcast and future projections) up by a constant amount to align the observed and modeled 1981–2014 means. The project team did this for annual average as well as each of the four seasons. The annual average model outputs shifted up by approximately 0.33 million square miles.

8. Display

The interactive graph for this pairing shows the following elements:

  • Observed data from 1981 to 2023.
  • Modeled hindcast from 1950 to 2014. The line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 13 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted from 1955 to 2009, as the project team did not attempt to apply any endpoint padding at either end of the series.
  • Modeled projections from 2015 to 2100 for four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), with 2014 added for continuity (2014 is the last year before the scenarios diverge). Each scenario line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 13 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted starting at 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast annual ranges, although the scenarios do not start to diverge until 2015. Smoothed values for 2014–2019 pick up some hindcast years in the average. The 11-year means are plotted through 2095, including data from 2090 through 2100, the last year of available data. Scenarios have been assigned “plain-language” names for consistency throughout this pairings effort.
  • A shaded band around each of the scenarios, reflecting the 10th to 90th percentiles among the 16 models. This shaded band therefore illustrates the range of modeled values. The shaded bands show annual values; they have not been smoothed. The projected ranges start in 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast, but the scenarios begin to diverge in 2015.

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

The technical documentation for the Snow Cover indicator provides citations and links for quality assurance and quality control measures that occur throughout the analytical process for the observed data, particularly in GSL’s filtering and correction steps. Through its review, GSL helps to provide objective third-party verification of NOAA data. Quality procedures for each GCM (e.g., validation) are described in source papers published by the organizations that have developed and run each model, available through the links in the overall technical documentation [to be linked] for this effort. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
